usage: go safely / take care on the way
examples: the plain polite goodbye to the leaver
shop staff: pairs with 또 오세요
Take care on the way, teacher. Goodbye.
student stays as the teacher leaves; 살펴 가세요 is extra-respectful
nuance: 안녕히 가세요 is the goodbye you say to the person who is LEAVING while you remain. 안녕(安寧) is Sino-Korean for 'peace, well-being', 히 makes it adverbial ('peacefully'), and 가세요 is the polite command of 가다 'to go' — so the whole thing literally wishes them 'go in peace'. The decisive contrast is with its twin 안녕히 계세요 (계시다 'to stay'): the verb tells you who moves. The English-speaker pitfall is huge: English 'goodbye' is one word for both parties, so learners fire 안녕히 가세요 at the person they are leaving behind, which sounds like ordering your host out of their own home. Decide first: am I going, or are they? If they go, 가세요. Softer caring versions are 조심히 가세요 and 살펴 가세요 ('go carefully'); the steeliest formal register is 안녕히 가십시오, heard from staff toward customers.

english: Goodbye (said by the person who is leaving).
usage: softening that you leave before them
bye, keep up the good work
examples: you depart, they stay; 먼저 갈게요 flags you leave early
바쁘신데 시간 내 주셔서 감사합니다. 안녕히 계세요.
Thank you for making time. Goodbye.
nuance: 안녕히 계세요 is the mirror image of 안녕히 가세요: you say it when YOU leave and the other person STAYS. The pivot is the verb — 계시다 is the honorific of 있다 'to be/stay (of a person)', so 계세요 wishes the one remaining to 'stay well', exactly as 가세요 (가다 'go') wishes the one leaving to 'go well'. A common smoothing move is to add 먼저 갈게요 / 먼저 가 볼게요 ('I'll go first') so leaving ahead of others doesn't seem abrupt. In a workplace, 안녕히 계세요 + 수고하세요 toward those still working is the natural exit line. Formal register: 안녕히 계십시오.

examples: Hello, nice to meet you. I'm Jimin.
I've heard a lot about you. Pleased to meet you.
formal first meeting after an introduction
nuance: 만나서 반가워요 = 만나서 ('because/upon meeting', from 만나다 + the -아서 link of cause) + 반가워요 (반갑다 'to be glad'). So it literally says 'I'm glad because I've met you'. Note 반갑다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: before 어요 the ㅂ becomes 우, giving 반가워요 (not 반갑어요) — the same shift you see in 춥다→추워요, 돕다→도와요. The synonym line worth knowing is 만나다 vs 보다: 만나다 is a planned, face-to-face meeting (so it suits a first introduction), whereas 보다 is broader 'see'. Register-wise 반가워요 is warm and friendly; 반갑습니다 is the buttoned-up formal version for business. The English-speaker pitfall is reusing it like a casual 'good to see you' on later meetings — Koreans say 만나서 반가워요 essentially for the FIRST encounter; at later meetings they switch to 오랜만이에요 or 잘 지냈어요?. The natural reply is 저도 반가워요 ('me too').

english: How do you do (formal first meeting).
usage: how do you do, I'm Minsu Kim
it's an honor to meet you
I look forward to working with you
examples: How do you do. I'm Minsu Kim. I look forward to working with you.
부장님, 처음 뵙겠습니다. 말씀 많이 들었습니다.
Director, how do you do. I've heard so much about you.
nuance: 처음 뵙겠습니다 is the high-formality greeting for meeting someone for the very FIRST time, especially in business. 처음 means 'first time'; 뵙다 (also written 뵈다) is the HUMBLE verb for 'to meet/see (a superior)', the lowered counterpart of plain 만나다/보다, so you are figuratively 'lowering yourself to be seen by' the other person. The -겠- here is not future 'will' but a softening, intention-marking 겠 that adds courtesy ('I shall (now) meet you'). Contrast with 만나서 반가워요: that conveys your emotion ('glad'), while 처음 뵙겠습니다 conveys deference and formality — Koreans often say both, the humble greeting first, then 반갑습니다. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like a casual 'hi, nice to meet you' and using it with friends or peers, where it sounds absurdly stiff and even sarcastic; reserve it for clients, executives, in-laws, and first formal introductions. It almost always pairs with 잘 부탁드립니다.

english: I will eat well (said before eating).
usage: I'll eat well (= thanks for the food)
examples: Thanks for the food. (lit. I'll eat well)
Wow, looks delicious. I'll eat well.
Thank you for preparing all this. I'll eat well.
thanking the host who set the table
nuance: 잘 먹겠습니다 is what you say JUST BEFORE eating, especially when someone has cooked for you or is treating you — functionally Korea's version of an at-the-table 'thank you for the food'. Structure: 잘 'well' + 먹다 'to eat' + the intention-marking -겠- ('I shall') + formal 습니다, so literally 'I shall eat well'. The crucial contrast is tense/aspect against its partner 잘 먹었습니다 (past, said AFTER finishing): -겠- looks forward, -었- looks back, and mixing them is the classic learner error. Casual register drops to 잘 먹을게요 or, among close friends, 잘 먹을게. A warmer variant aimed at the cook is 맛있게 먹겠습니다 ('I'll eat this deliciously'). The English-speaker pitfall is expecting it to mean a literal promise about how much/how skillfully you'll eat — it's a fixed courtesy formula, not a statement about appetite, and you say it even for a tiny snack someone offers.

usage: thanks, that was a great meal
examples: Thanks, that was great. (lit. I ate well)
It was really delicious. Thank you for the meal.
praising the food as you finish
사장님, 잘 먹었습니다. 다음엔 제가 대접할게요.
Thank you for the meal, boss. Next time it's my treat.
nuance: 잘 먹었습니다 is the AFTER-meal counterpart to 잘 먹겠습니다 — said as you finish, it thanks whoever cooked or paid, much like 'that was a wonderful meal'. The only structural change is tense: 먹다 + past -었- + 습니다 = 'I ate well', versus the pre-meal 먹겠습니다 with forward-looking -겠-. Note the vowel join: 먹 + 었 → 먹었습니다 (the ㄱ ㅓ stem takes 었 normally; pronounced 머거씀니다). Keeping the before/after pair straight (먹겠습니다 → 먹었습니다) is exactly the contrast learners stumble on. Casual register is 잘 먹었어요 or, with friends, 잘 먹었어. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as merely a factual report ('I have eaten') rather than a thank-you — so people forget to say it to the host, or say it to no one. It's customary to direct it to the cook/treater, and after being treated it pairs naturally with an offer like 다음엔 제가 살게요 ('I'll get the next one').

examples: Minsu, long time no see. Have you been well?
pairs with the 'how have you been' follow-up
어머, 이게 얼마 만이에요! 정말 오랜만이에요.
Oh my, how long has it been! It's been ages.
nuance: 오랜만이에요 is what you say when meeting someone after a long gap. It comes from 오래 'a long time' + 간만/만 'interval' contracted into 오랜만 (a span of time having passed), plus the polite copula 이에요 — literally 'it is (after) a long while'. Beware the spelling trap: it is 오랜만 (오래+ㄴ만), NOT 오랫만; many learners (and some natives) miswrite it. Register slides from casual 오랜만이야 → polite 오랜만이에요 → formal 오랜만입니다. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, 'long time no see' is broken English, so don't try to map it word-for-word — 오랜만이에요 is a normal, grammatical copula sentence; second, it requires a genuinely long gap, so using it after a few days sounds sarcastic (Koreans even joke '오랜만이네?' when they just saw you yesterday). It naturally leads into 잘 지냈어요? ('have you been well?'), and a common echo reply is 그러게요, 오랜만이에요.

examples: Long time no see. How have you been all this time?
저는 잘 지내요. 민수 씨는 어떻게 지내세요?
I'm doing well. And how about you, Minsu?
answering, then returning the question honorifically
nuance: 어떻게 지내요? asks how someone has been LIVING/getting on lately — a span of life — not how they feel this exact second. 어떻게 = 'how', 지내다 = 'to get by / spend one's days', so it's closer to 'How have you been getting on?' than a snapshot 'How do you feel now?'. The synonym contrast: 어떻게 지내요? is open-ended ('in what way are you living?'), while 잘 지내요? is a yes/no-style 'Are you doing well?' that fishes for the reassuring 네, 잘 지내요. Register climbs with the honorific 지내시다 → 어떻게 지내세요? for seniors. It frequently follows 오랜만이에요 at reunions, and you can shift it to the past 어떻게 지냈어요? to mean 'how have you been (since we last met)'. The English-speaker pitfall is parsing 지내요 as 'go' (confusing it with 가요) and answering about a destination; 지내다 is about how life is going, not where you're headed — answer with 잘 지내요 / 그냥 그래요 ('so-so'), not a place.

examples: Congrats on graduating! You really worked hard.
occasion goes in front: 졸업 + 축하해요
Director, my sincere congratulations on your promotion.
nuance: 축하해요 congratulates someone on good news. 축하(祝賀) is Sino-Korean — 祝 'to wish/celebrate' + 賀 'to congratulate' — and it's a 하다-verb (축하 + 하다), so it conjugates 축하하다 → 축하해요, with the casual 축하해 and formal 축하합니다. The pattern is [occasion] + 축하해요: 졸업 축하해요, 합격 축하해요, 결혼 축하해요. A key register note: toward a senior, Koreans prefer the humble 축하드려요/축하드립니다 (드리다 'to give (humbly)') over plain 축하해요, because you are respectfully 'offering' the congratulation. The English-speaker pitfall is using it like the broad English 'congratulations' for any achievement-y moment including consolation — in Korean 축하해요 is strictly for genuinely happy events (births, weddings, jobs, awards). For sympathy or hardship you do NOT congratulate; you'd say something like 힘내세요 ('stay strong') or 고생했어요. Also don't confuse it with 화이팅 (cheering someone ON before an event); 축하해요 is for celebrating AFTER good news lands.

usage: formal, or to a peer at work
examples: 민수 씨, 생일 축하해요. 좋은 하루 보내요!
Minsu, happy birthday. Have a great day!
honorific 생신 + 축하드리다 for an elder

english: Thank you for your hard work.
usage: thank you for your hard work
formal, after the work is done
to someone STILL working (often as you leave)
examples: Thank you for your hard work.
Thanks for your work in today's meeting. See you tomorrow.
after a finished task, past form
I'll head home first. Keep up the good work.
present 수고하세요 to colleagues still working
nuance: 수고하셨습니다 thanks someone for effort that is FINISHED. 수고 means 'trouble, effort, hard work', 하시— is the honorific stem of 하다 'to do', and the past -셨- marks completion, so it's 'you have done hard work'. The make-or-break contrast is tense: past 수고하셨습니다 (the job is over) vs present 수고하세요 (the person is still at it, said as you leave them to it) — pick by whether the work has ended. A warm near-synonym is 고생하셨습니다 (고생 'hardship'), which feels a touch more heartfelt about the toil endured. The big register caution for English speakers: 수고하셨습니다 is best from a senior/peer DOWN or sideways; saying it UPWARD to a clearly higher-ranking boss can sound presumptuous (as if you are evaluating their effort), so to a superior prefer 감사합니다 or 고생 많으셨습니다 with care. The pitfall is using the wrong tense (telling someone whose work is done to 'keep working', or telling someone still working that they 'have finished'), and treating it as a casual 'thanks' you can drop on anyone of any rank.

examples: It's late. See you tomorrow, good night.
할머니, 안녕히 주무세요. 좋은 꿈 꾸세요.
nuance: 잘 자요 = 잘 'well' + 자다 'to sleep' in polite command form, literally 'sleep well'. Here's the subtlety: 잘 자요 is friendly-polite, but it's the 해요체 of a fairly intimate phrase, so it lands best with peers, friends, and partners — it is NOT respectful enough for elders or superiors. For them you switch to a completely different, honorific verb: 주무시다 (the honorific of 자다), giving 안녕히 주무세요 ('please sleep peacefully'). This verb-swapping for respect (자다 → 주무시다, just like 먹다 → 드시다, 있다 → 계시다) is the heart of the lesson. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'good night' as one neutral phrase for everyone and saying 잘 자요 to a boss, in-law, or grandparent, which sounds far too familiar — almost like telling your CEO to 'sleep tight'. Decide by relationship: intimate/peer → 잘 자(요); elder/superior → 안녕히 주무세요. A warm add-on for either register is 좋은 꿈 꿔요 / 꾸세요 ('sweet dreams').
